reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Represents target-organ resistance to parathyroid hormone rather than a deficiency, so hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia coexist with elevated PTH
The biochemical signature (low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH, normal renal function) distinguishes it from true hypoparathyroidism where PTH is low
The type 1a phenotype is associated with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features such as short stature, rounded face, obesity, and shortened fourth and fifth metacarpals
Resistance is often multi-hormonal because the same signalling defect can blunt responses to TSH and gonadotropins, so hypothyroidism may accompany it
Genomic imprinting explains why the same genetic defect produces full hormone resistance or only the skeletal phenotype (pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism) depending on parental origin
Chronic hypocalcaemia may cause tetany, paraesthesiae, seizures, and basal ganglia calcification
Management centres on correcting calcium and vitamin D status while monitoring phosphate, calcium, and PTH over the long term
Family evaluation is important because inheritance patterns and imprinting influence expression across relatives
reference.pathophysiology: Pseudohypoparathyroidism arises from impaired signal transduction downstream of the PTH receptor, most commonly through defects in the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit (GNAS) that couples receptors to adenylate cyclase. Renal tubules therefore fail to respond to PTH, reducing phosphate excretion and impairing activation of vitamin D, which lowers serum calcium. The resulting hypocalcaemia drives compensatory secretion of PTH, so levels are high despite the biochemical picture of hormone deficiency. Because GNAS is subject to genomic imprinting and couples several hormone receptors, the clinical phenotype varies from isolated skeletal features to combined resistance affecting thyroid and gonadal axes.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Other causes of hypocalcaemia such as acute pancreatitis
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium, and intact PTH
25-hydroxyvitamin D and renal function to exclude other causes
Thyroid function tests to detect associated TSH resistance
Radiographs of the hands for metacarpal shortening and skeletal features
Brain imaging where basal ganglia calcification is suspected
Genetic and GNAS methylation analysis to confirm the subtype
redFlags: Severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, laryngospasm, or seizures requiring urgent calcium correction
Cardiac features of hypocalcaemia such as QT prolongation and arrhythmia
Untreated associated hypothyroidism, especially in infancy affecting neurodevelopment
reference.prognosis: With calcium and active vitamin D replacement, most patients maintain acceptable calcium levels and avoid acute complications, though the skeletal and metabolic features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy and any associated hormone resistance persist and require lifelong follow-up.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the disorder as true hypoparathyroidism by not measuring PTH
Overlooking associated thyroid or gonadal resistance
Failing to correct coexisting hypomagnesaemia, which can perpetuate hypocalcaemia
Missing the diagnosis in relatives with subtle or imprinting-dependent phenotypes
